clue.text: Schizophrenic sort of headache?

explanation.surface: A question whether a mental disorder might be a kind of headache.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses of one word: the popular idea of schizophrenia as a divided mind, and the stock adjective for a really bad headache.
explanation.definitionFit: A schizophrenic is popularly said to have a divided personality, and a severe, pounding headache is described as one that feels like it is cracking the skull apart.

clue.text: Eleven children? That's relatively unimportant

parts.note: a cricket or football team of eleven players is a side
issue means offspring, children

explanation.surface: A remark that having eleven kids is not a big deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eleven' is a team, a side, in cricket or football; 'children' is issue, the legal word for offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: A side issue is a secondary matter, a point of lesser importance next to the main question.

clue.text: Clumsy oafs striking in the fifties

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty, so fifties are two Ls
workers who are striking are out

explanation.surface: Ungainly thugs taking industrial action back in the 1950s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the fifties' looks like the decade; it is two Ls, Roman fifties, with OUT (on strike) 'in' them. 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Louts are rough, uncouth young men, boorish and awkward oafs.

clue.text: Clever if explosive journalist drinking beer

indicators.note: one piece drinks the other, taking it inside

parts.note: TNT is the explosive trinitrotoluene
ale is a kind of beer
ED is short for editor, the stock crossword journalist

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a hot-tempered reporter knocking back beer can be bright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'explosive' looks like it describes the journalist's temper, but it names the explosive itself; 'drinking' puts the beer inside that, ahead of the editor. 'if' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Talented means gifted, having natural ability, so it is a fair stand-in for clever.

clue.text: Announce a great friend

explanation.surface: Proclaiming a close companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words of the same spelling, said differently: the verb (ending '-mate') means to hint or make known, the noun (ending '-mət') is a close friend.
explanation.definitionFit: To intimate is to make known or hint at; an intimate is a very close friend or confidant.

clue.text: Note cut or other stroke

parts.note: G is a note in the musical scale
to lance is to cut, as a surgeon lances a boil

explanation.surface: Cricket talk: a cut shot or some other stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a cut is itself a stroke, which tempts you to read 'cut or other stroke' as the definition. A glance is the stroke deflecting the ball off the bat's face to fine leg.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the glance is a delicate shot deflecting the ball behind the wicket, another of the batsman's shots.

clue.text: Leading Tory's written about one subject

indicators.note: the first group of letters is written around the next piece, so it encloses it

parts.note: leading means top, foremost
C stands for Conservative, the party of the Tories
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A senior Conservative has written about a single subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading Tory' looks like one person, the T of Tory; it is really two pieces, TOP and C, and 'written about' puts I inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is the theme or matter under discussion, the same as a subject.

clue.text: Town house my errant love frequents

definitions.text: Town house my errant love frequents

parts.words: Town house my errant love frequents
parts.note: house is read as a public house in town, and the wayward lover is a regular drinker there rather than a resident

explanation.surface: A grand house in town that an unfaithful lover keeps visiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Town house' suggests a smart city residence, perhaps a secret love nest; it is really a pub, the place where a drinker spends evenings.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn or pub is a public house where drinkers gather, the haunt of a straying partner.

clue.text: Maybe 26 on a horse

parts.note: the answer to 26, a cockerel, is one example of a bird that sits on a perch
taken as written

explanation.surface: Perhaps the answer to 26 sitting astride a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is ROOSTER, which perches, so it is a PERCHER; add ON. The Percheron is a big French draught horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Percheron is a breed of heavy draught horse from the Perche region of France.

clue.text: "Greet the unseen with a —" (Browning)

parts.note: a gap in a quotation to fill: the last word of a line from Robert Browning's Epilogue to Asolando

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank line from a Victorian poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's Epilogue to Asolando closes with 'Greet the unseen with a cheer!'; there is no wordplay, just the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's line asks the reader to meet the unknown with a shout of encouragement and good spirits.

clue.text: Old garment for the Manx race

explanation.surface: A period costume worn for the famous motorcycle race on the Isle of Man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man's motorbike race is the TT, a letter T written twice, so it is a 'double T'. The other sense is the close-fitting jacket men wore in Tudor times.
explanation.definitionFit: A doublet is a man's close-fitting Renaissance jacket; the Manx TT race is named by two Ts, a pair of that letter.

clue.text: Opposed a rhyming poster?

parts.note: a poster is an advertisement, AD for short
rhyming lines make verse

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they are against a poster written in rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: An advertising poster in rhyme would be 'ad verse', which runs together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse means hostile or contrary, as in an adverse opinion that is set against something.

clue.text: Retired dramatist supplied Jane's big part

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the letters run backwards
the letters come from part of the words Jane's big

explanation.surface: A retired playwright gave Jane a large role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part' takes NESBI from 'Jane's big', and 'Retired' turns it backwards. 'Retired' looks like a description of the playwright but is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian playwright of A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler.

clue.text: General finds skill in the R.A. much changed

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the middle of the other
these letters are greatly altered, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the R.A. is the Royal Academy, RA
art is skill, as in the art of cooking

explanation.surface: A military man discovers some talent at the Royal Academy, which has altered a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'much changed' rearranges the letters of the academy's initials plus 'much' into MACHUR, and 'in' puts the skill inside. 'the' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas MacArthur was the American five-star general who commanded in the Pacific in the Second World War.

clue.text: So many openings that provide solutions

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty, a crossword stand-in for many
vents are openings, holes letting air or gas out

explanation.surface: So many gaps that offer the answers.
explanation.walkthrough: Using L, fifty, for 'many' is a crossword convention. The 'solutions' are liquids with something dissolved in them, not answers.
explanation.definitionFit: A solvent dissolves a substance, producing a chemical solution of it in liquid.

clue.text: So our bail is dislodged -how 27!

indicators.note: dislodged means knocked out of place, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Cricket scene: the bail has been knocked off, and how slow it all is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dislodged' rearranges SO OUR BAIL. In cricket the bails sit on top of the stumps and are knocked off when a batsman is bowled. 27 is OPEROSE, a rare word for wearisome effort, so the answer is the 'how' of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Laborious and operose are synonyms, both meaning toilsome and needing great effort.

clue.text: Food supplied by Gabriel, Pickwickian sexton

explanation.surface: Food handed out by a gravedigger from a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Gabriel Grub is the grumpy sexton (a church caretaker who digs graves) in a ghost story told in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Grub is informal slang for food, and Gabriel Grub is the surname of the goblin-haunted gravedigger in Dickens's Pickwick Papers.

clue.text: Dolt features in ancient execution

explanation.surface: A fool shows up in a historical beheading.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the word as its two parts: a beheading in old times needed a chopping block and a head.
explanation.definitionFit: A blockhead is a stupid person; and a block and a head are the things that featured when the executioner's axe fell.

clue.text: The local authority?

parts.note: local is read as the neighbourhood pub, so the authority there is the person who runs it, not the town council

explanation.surface: A question about the town council.
explanation.walkthrough: A British 'local' is a nearby pub, and the person in charge of it is its keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: The publican, who runs and licenses a pub, holds authority over the bar and its customers.

clue.text: Very close is a record-spinner with a bit of money

parts.note: a disc jockey spins records, a DJ
a cent is a small coin, a hundredth of a dollar

explanation.surface: A remark that a disc jockey is near to having some cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' and 'with' are only links joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjacent means lying next to or bordering, right alongside, so very near indeed.

clue.text: Declines to expose a rock group?

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to unmask a band of rock musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'rock group' is not a band: it is a cluster of rocks on the shore, uncovered when the tide goes out.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebbs means dwindles or falls away; when the tide ebbs it draws back and leaves rocks on the shore uncovered.

clue.text: Dance by devotee before Dagon perhaps

parts.note: a devotee is a fan, an enthusiast

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the word Dagon might be in some other form, so it is rearranged

explanation.surface: A dance performed by a worshipper in front of the Philistine god Dagon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the god's name into DANGO, which follows the devotee as 'before' says. Dagon was a god of the Philistines in the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The fandango is a lively Spanish courtship dance in triple time, done with castanets.

clue.text: Animals Tom let out

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

indicators.note: out signals letters knocked out of place, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Tom lets the animals out of the pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a name; it is a tomcat, CAT. 'out' rearranges LET into TLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle are cows and bulls, livestock kept on farms.

clue.text: Wood gets butter for Indian hermitage

parts.note: ash is a tree and its timber
a ram butts with its head, so it is a butter

explanation.surface: A tree gets a spread of dairy fat for a religious retreat in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is not the spread but one who butts, a RAM. 'gets' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashram is a secluded religious community or retreat in India, the home of a guru.

clue.text: Excelled on translation and satisfied examiners

parts.note: sur is French for on, so on translated gives it
a candidate who satisfied the examiners passed

explanation.surface: A student did brilliantly on a translation paper and got through the exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on translation' means the word on put into French, SUR; the surface makes it sound like a translation test.
explanation.definitionFit: To surpass is to go beyond or outdo, so surpassed means did better than all others.

clue.text: Sagacious tailless animal

indicators.note: without its tail, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: sagacious means wise, shrewd

explanation.surface: A wise creature that has no tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' looks as though it describes the animal; it cuts the final D from SHREWD.
explanation.definitionFit: The shrew is a small mouse-like mammal with a long pointed snout.

clue.text: Expression of regret for a deficiency

parts.note: a deficiency is a lack, a shortage

explanation.surface: Words of sorrow for a shortfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is only a link joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Alack is an archaic exclamation of sorrow, as in 'alas and alack'.

clue.text: Concerning a vessel turning up empty

annotationWithheld.why: Concerning a vessel turning up empty (5): A + reversed TUB with O inside (BOUT); 'empty' must both supply O (nothing) and signal its insertion, one word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Concerning a vessel turning up empty

clue.text: What crew on Hook's ship? sounded like this

definitions.text: What crew on Hook's ship? sounded like this

parts.words: What crew on Hook's ship? sounded like this
parts.note: crew is read as the past tense of crow, so the clue asks which creature crowed like this, with Hook's pirate ship as the false scene

explanation.surface: A question about the noise made by the pirate crew aboard Captain Hook's ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crew' looks like the ship's sailors; it is the old past tense of crow, and the cockerel is the one that crowed. The italics tell you the second half is to be read differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A cock bird famously crows at dawn, so it is the creature that 'crew'.

clue.text: Nothing in itself about love is tedious

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing

indicators.note: the Latin phrase goes around the next piece, enclosing it

parts.note: per se is Latin for in itself
love is zero in tennis, O

explanation.surface: A remark that nothing about love is, by its nature, boring.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase for 'in itself' goes 'about' love (a zero score in tennis), after the zero for 'Nothing'. The answer is a rare word.
explanation.definitionFit: Operose is a rare literary word for laborious, demanding much effort and so wearisome.

clue.text: Unused part of the body, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken, giving one that sounds the same

parts.note: the waist is the part of the body between ribs and hips

explanation.surface: A question whether an unused bit of the anatomy counts as part of the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' means the word for a part of the body is spoken, giving a different spelling with the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Waste land or waste material is left unused, not put to any productive purpose.

clue.text: Considered it might be heartless to have intervened

annotationWithheld.why: Considered it might be heartless to have intervened (9): MEDITATED, whose heart (the central T) removed gives MEDIATED; the T comes from the answer itself, not any clue word, so the grammar cannot express it
annotationWithheld.clue: Considered it might be heartless to have intervened
